title: OA 1 — Foundations (Easy)
description: Easy mock data-science internship assessment: CS/AI/ML/statistics/testing MCQs, aptitude, chart-based data analysis, SQL, pandas and DSA.
disclaimer: Independent practice material informed by publicly reported role requirements and general internship-assessment patterns. Not official Nasdaq questions.

revealPolicy.rule: Never send private fields to the candidate before the whole attempt has finished.

sections.title: Section 1: CS Fundamentals, AI, ML, Statistics and Testing

questions.statement: A depth-unrestricted decision tree predicting next-day volume has a training RMSE of 0.4 and a validation RMSE of 3.9. Which action is the most appropriate first step?

options.text: Report the training RMSE because it is the lower and therefore better estimate
Remove the validation set so the model can use more data for training
Constrain the model (e.g., limit tree depth or require a minimum leaf size) and re-check validation error
Add more tree depth so training error becomes exactly zero

solution.explanation: A large train/validation gap signals high variance (overfitting). Restricting model capacity or adding regularization usually narrows the gap. Making the tree deeper would worsen it; training error is an optimistic estimate and must not be reported as performance.

hints: Large gap between training error and validation error is the classic sign of overfitting — think about limiting model capacity.

questions.statement: Which model's predictions are least affected if every numeric feature is multiplied by a different positive constant (feature rescaling)?

options.text: A decision tree, because splits depend only on the ordering of feature values
Ridge regression, because the penalty is applied per example
A support vector machine with an RBF kernel
k-nearest neighbours, because distances are scale invariant

solution.explanation: Trees choose thresholds on single features, so positive rescaling only moves the thresholds. Distance-based models (kNN, RBF-SVM) change which points are near; penalised linear models change how much each coefficient is penalised.

hints: Which model only compares feature values with thresholds, rather than computing distances or penalties?

questions.statement: A fraud model outputs probabilities. The risk team says missing a real fraud case is far more costly than reviewing a legitimate one. What should happen to the classification threshold, and what is the typical consequence?

options.text: Raise the threshold: recall rises and precision usually falls
Lower the threshold: recall rises and precision usually falls
Lower the threshold: precision rises and recall usually falls
Keep 0.5, since the threshold has no effect on recall

solution.explanation: Flagging more cases (lower cut-off) catches more true frauds (higher recall) at the cost of more false positives (lower precision). Raising the threshold does the opposite.

hints: Lower threshold → more cases flagged. Which of precision/recall benefits from flagging more?

questions.statement: Which of the following is a classification problem?

options.text: Predicting tomorrow's closing price of a stock as a number
Estimating the number of customers who will visit next week
Predicting the temperature in degrees Celsius
Deciding whether an incoming transaction is fraudulent or legitimate

solution.explanation: Classification predicts a discrete label (fraud / not fraud). The other options predict continuous numeric values, which is regression.

hints: Classification predicts a category/label; regression predicts a number.

questions.statement: Why is a dataset usually split into training and test sets?

options.text: To remove noisy rows from the data
To estimate how well the model performs on data it has not seen during training
To make the model train faster on a smaller dataset only
To guarantee that the model will never overfit

solution.explanation: A held-out test set gives an honest estimate of generalisation. Splitting does not guarantee absence of overfitting; it only lets you detect it.

hints: Ask: on which data can you honestly measure performance on 'unseen' cases?

questions.statement: A regression model makes prediction errors of 1, −2 and 3 on three test points. What is the mean squared error (MSE)?

solution.explanation: MSE = (1² + (−2)² + 3²)/3 = 14/3 ≈ 4.67. The mean of the signed errors is 0.67 and the mean absolute error is 2; 2.16 is the RMSE (√4.67).

hints: MSE = (sum of squared errors) / n. Square each error first: 1, 4, 9.

questions.statement: You are building a model at market close to predict whether tomorrow's closing price will be higher than today's. One candidate feature is 'tomorrow's total traded volume'. What is the correct decision?

options.text: Include it but standardise it so the leakage has less effect
Exclude it: it is not available at prediction time, so it leaks future information and will inflate offline metrics
Include it only in the training set and leave it out of the test set
Include it: more predictive features always improve the model

solution.explanation: A feature must be computable at the moment of prediction. Tomorrow's volume is only known after the target period, so offline scores would be unrealistically good and the model would fail in production. Scaling or train-only inclusion does not fix leakage.

hints: Can you know tomorrow's volume at the moment you must make the prediction?

questions.statement: A random sample of n = 64 order latencies has mean 12.0 ms and sample standard deviation 8.0 ms. Using the normal approximation, what is an approximate 95% confidence interval for the true mean latency?

solution.explanation: SE = 8/√64 = 1, so the interval is 12 ± 1.96·1 = (10.04, 13.96). (4.16, 19.84) wrongly uses the standard deviation instead of the standard error; (8.08, 15.92) uses SE = 2 (n=16).

hints: 95% CI ≈ mean ± 1.96 × (s / √n). Compute the standard error first.

questions.statement: A random variable X (daily P&L in thousands) has E[X] = 4 and Var(X) = 9. What are the mean and variance of Y = 2X + 3?

solution.explanation: E[2X+3] = 2·4 + 3 = 11. Adding a constant does not change variance and scaling by 2 multiplies variance by 2² = 4, so Var(Y) = 4·9 = 36.

hints: E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b and Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X) (adding a constant does not change variance).

questions.statement: For two events: P(Flagged) = 0.30, P(High-value) = 0.50 and P(Flagged and High-value) = 0.15. Which statement is correct?

options.text: They are mutually exclusive, because 0.15 is small
They are independent, because P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B) = 0.15
They are independent because P(A) + P(B) < 1
They are dependent, because P(A∩B) is not zero

solution.explanation: Independence means P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B); here 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15. Mutually exclusive events would have P(A∩B) = 0 (and are then dependent, unless one has probability 0).

hints: Events are independent exactly when P(A∩B) = P(A) × P(B).

questions.statement: In a simple linear regression of one stock's return on another's, the sample correlation is r = 0.8. What is R²?

solution.explanation: In simple linear regression R² = r² = 0.64: 64% of the variance of the response is explained by the predictor. √0.8 ≈ 0.89 is a common mistake.

hints: In simple linear regression, R² = r².

questions.statement: A monitoring rule fires a false alarm with probability 0.10 each day, independently. What is the probability of at least one false alarm in 5 days?

solution.explanation: P(no alarm in 5 days) = 0.9⁵ ≈ 0.59, so P(at least one) ≈ 0.41. Adding probabilities (5 × 0.1) ignores overlap and overstates the result.

hints: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none) = 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ.

questions.statement: In a test of whether a new fraud rule changes the alert rate, you obtain p = 0.03. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: If the rule truly had no effect, results at least as extreme as those observed would occur about 3% of the time
There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true
There is a 97% probability that the rule works

solution.explanation: A p-value is computed assuming H0 is true: P(data this extreme | H0). It is not the probability that H0 is true or that the alternative holds, and it says nothing about effect magnitude.

hints: A p-value is computed assuming the null hypothesis is true — it is NOT the probability that the null is true.

questions.statement: A team has two years of unlabelled order-flow records and wants to discover groups of traders with similar behaviour. Which approach fits?

options.text: Supervised regression to predict trader IDs
Supervised classification with logistic regression, since logistic regression works on any dataset
Unsupervised learning, e.g., k-means or hierarchical clustering on behavioural features
Reinforcement learning, since there is a reward in every trade

solution.explanation: With no labels and an exploratory goal of finding structure, clustering is the natural tool. Logistic regression needs labelled targets; there is no sequential decision problem or reward signal specified for reinforcement learning.

hints: No labels → which family of methods finds groups on its own?

questions.statement: While training a neural network, training loss keeps decreasing but validation loss starts increasing after epoch 12. What is the standard remedy?

options.text: Evaluate only on the training data from now on
Increase the learning rate to reduce the training loss faster
Stop at (or restore weights from) about epoch 12 – early stopping – and/or add regularization such as dropout
Train for many more epochs until the validation loss comes down by itself

solution.explanation: Diverging validation loss indicates overfitting. Early stopping and regularization limit memorisation; training longer or ignoring validation performance makes it worse.

hints: Training keeps improving while validation worsens → overfitting → stop earlier or regularise.

questions.statement: Two embedding vectors are u = (3, 4) and v = (4, 3). What is their cosine similarity?

solution.explanation: u·v = 12 + 12 = 24 and |u||v| = 5·5 = 25, so cos = 24/25 = 0.96. It would be 1 only for vectors pointing in the same direction.

hints: cos θ = (u·v) / (|u| |v|). Dot product 3·4 + 4·3, lengths 5 and 5.

questions.statement: A weight has value 2.0, the gradient of the loss with respect to it is 0.5, and the learning rate is 0.1. After one gradient-descent step what is the weight?

solution.explanation: w ← w − η·∇L = 2.0 − 0.1·0.5 = 1.95. Gradient descent moves against the gradient.

hints: w_new = w − learning_rate × gradient.

questions.statement: Which statement about A* search is correct?

options.text: A* ignores the cost already paid and ranks nodes only by the heuristic
A* always expands fewer nodes than breadth-first search regardless of the heuristic
With an admissible heuristic (one that never overestimates the true remaining cost) A* returns a lowest-cost path
A* is optimal for any heuristic as long as it is non-negative

solution.explanation: A* orders nodes by f = g + h. If h is admissible (and the graph search is handled consistently), the first goal popped is optimal. A non-negative but overestimating heuristic can mislead the search; ranking only by h is greedy best-first search, which is not optimal.

hints: A* ranks nodes by f = g + h. What must h never do to keep the answer optimal?

questions.statement: Table P(price) contains the values 10, NULL, 20, NULL, 30. What does SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(price), AVG(price) FROM P return?

solution.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows (5); COUNT(price) ignores NULLs (3); AVG ignores NULLs, so (10+20+30)/3 = 20, not 60/5 = 12.

hints: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) and AVG(col) skip NULLs.

questions.statement: A funds transfer runs two UPDATEs (debit account A, credit account B). The system crashes after the first UPDATE but before the second. Which ACID property ensures the debit is rolled back?

solution.explanation: Atomicity means a transaction is all-or-nothing: if it cannot complete, its partial changes are undone. Isolation concerns concurrent transactions; durability guarantees that committed data survives crashes.

hints: ACID: which letter means 'all or nothing'?

hints: Both operands are int, so division happens in integers BEFORE the assignment to double.

questions.statement: An order-entry rule accepts quantities from 1 to 1,000 inclusive. Which set of test inputs best applies boundary value analysis?

solution.explanation: Defects cluster at the edges, so test just outside and exactly on each boundary: 0 and 1 for the lower edge, 1000 and 1001 for the upper edge. Mid-range values add little boundary coverage.

hints: Boundary value analysis tests just outside and exactly on each edge.

questions.statement: A KYC form accepts ages 18–65 inclusive. Using equivalence partitioning, what is the minimum number of test cases to cover every equivalence class (one representative each)?

solution.explanation: There are three classes: invalid-low, valid, invalid-high; each class needs one representative. Boundary-value analysis would add edge cases (17, 18, 65, 66) on top of this.

hints: Count the groups: below the range, inside the range, above the range.

questions.statement: What is the main difference between unit testing and integration testing?

options.text: Unit tests run only in production
Unit tests are manual and integration tests are automated
Integration tests check only the user interface
Unit tests check one small component in isolation; integration tests check that several components work together

solution.explanation: Unit tests exercise the smallest testable parts (functions/classes) with dependencies stubbed; integration tests verify the interactions between modules, services or databases.

hints: Unit = one component alone; integration = components interacting.

questions.title: Busiest Traders
questions.statement:
The operations team wants to know which traders are most active.

Using the `Trades` table, count only trades whose `status` is `'FILLED'`. For each trader who has **at least 2** filled trades return:

`trader_id, filled_trades, total_shares`

* `filled_trades` – number of filled trades
* `total_shares` – the sum of `quantity` over those trades

Sort by `total_shares` from highest to lowest; if two traders have the same total, the smaller `trader_id` comes first.
questions.schemaSql:
CREATE TABLE Trades (
  trade_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  security_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  trader_id   INTEGER NOT NULL,
  trade_date  TEXT NOT NULL,          -- 'YYYY-MM-DD'
  side        TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (side IN ('BUY','SELL')),
  quantity    INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
  price       REAL NOT NULL,
  status      TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('FILLED','PENDING','REJECTED','CANCELLED'))
);
questions.starterQuery:
SELECT trader_id, COUNT(*) AS filled_trades, SUM(quantity) AS total_shares
FROM Trades
-- TODO: keep only FILLED trades, then GROUP BY / HAVING / ORDER BY
GROUP BY trader_id;
questions.outputSpec: Columns, in order: trader_id, filled_trades, total_shares. Ordered by total_shares DESC, trader_id ASC.

hiddenTests.description: No trader has two filled trades (empty result)
hiddenTests.dataSql:
INSERT INTO Trades VALUES (1, 1, 7, '2024-03-01', 'BUY', 10, 5.0, 'FILLED');
INSERT INTO Trades VALUES (2, 1, 8, '2024-03-01', 'SELL', 10, 5.0, 'PENDING');

hiddenTests.description: Tie on total_shares broken by trader_id

solution.referenceSolution:
SELECT trader_id,
       COUNT(*)      AS filled_trades,
       SUM(quantity) AS total_shares
FROM Trades
WHERE status = 'FILLED'
GROUP BY trader_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY total_shares DESC, trader_id ASC;
solution.explanation: WHERE keeps FILLED rows only; GROUP BY trader_id builds one row per trader; HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 removes traders with a single filled trade; ORDER BY applies the requested ranking.

rubric.formula: earned = 100 * (sum of weights of passed tests) / (sum of all test weights)
rules: A submission that only compiles/executes without matching expected output earns 0 for that test.
A crash, syntax error or timeout fails only the affected test; remaining tests are still scored.
Filtering on status must happen before grouping (WHERE).
HAVING is needed for the 'at least 2' rule.
Tie-break ordering is tested.

questions.walkthrough: Only FILLED trades count, so trades 5, 8, 9, 10, 11 (PENDING) and 12 (CANCELLED) are ignored. Trader 101 has filled trades 1, 2 and 6 → 100 + 50 + 300 = 450 shares. Trader 102 has trades 3 and 4 → 200 + 100 = 300. Trader 104 has only one filled trade (7), so HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 removes it. Ordered by total_shares: 101, then 102.
hints: Which rows should be counted at all? Remove the others with WHERE before grouping.
GROUP BY trader_id gives one row per trader; COUNT(*) and SUM(quantity) are computed per group.
A condition on an aggregate (COUNT(*) >= 2) cannot go in WHERE — use HAVING. Finish with ORDER BY total_shares DESC, trader_id.

questions.title: Notional Traded per Ticker
questions.statement:
Using `Securities` and `Trades`, report how much value has been traded in each security.

Consider only trades with `status = 'FILLED'`. The **notional** of a trade is `quantity * price`. Return one row for every security that has at least one filled trade:

`ticker, filled_trades, total_notional`

* `filled_trades` – number of filled trades
* `total_notional` – the sum of the notionals, rounded to 2 decimals

Sort by `total_notional` descending, then `ticker` ascending.
questions.schemaSql:
CREATE TABLE Securities (
  security_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  ticker      TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name        TEXT NOT NULL,
  sector      TEXT NOT NULL,
  exchange    TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE MarketQuotes (
  quote_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  security_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Securities(security_id),
  quote_date  TEXT NOT NULL,          -- 'YYYY-MM-DD'
  bid         REAL,                   -- may be NULL (missing)
  ask         REAL,                   -- may be NULL (missing)
  volume      INTEGER NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE (security_id, quote_date)
);
CREATE TABLE Trades (
  trade_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  security_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Securities(security_id),
  trader_id   INTEGER NOT NULL,
  trade_date  TEXT NOT NULL,          -- 'YYYY-MM-DD'
  side        TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (side IN ('BUY','SELL')),
  quantity    INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
  price       REAL NOT NULL,
  status      TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('FILLED','PENDING','REJECTED','CANCELLED'))
);
questions.starterQuery:
SELECT s.ticker, COUNT(*) AS filled_trades, 0.0 AS total_notional
FROM Securities s
JOIN Trades t ON t.security_id = s.security_id
-- TODO: filter, aggregate notional, order
GROUP BY s.ticker;
questions.outputSpec: Columns, in order: ticker, filled_trades, total_notional. Ordered by total_notional DESC, ticker ASC.

hiddenTests.description: No filled trades at all (empty result)
A security with trades that are all cancelled is excluded

solution.referenceSolution:
SELECT s.ticker,
       COUNT(*)                              AS filled_trades,
       ROUND(SUM(t.quantity * t.price), 2)   AS total_notional
FROM Securities s
JOIN Trades t ON t.security_id = s.security_id
WHERE t.status = 'FILLED'
GROUP BY s.security_id, s.ticker
ORDER BY total_notional DESC, s.ticker ASC;
solution.explanation: Join each trade to its security, keep FILLED rows, multiply quantity by price for every row inside SUM, group per security and sort.

rubric.formula: earned = 200 * (sum of weights of passed tests) / (sum of all test weights)
rules: A submission that only compiles/executes without matching expected output earns 0 for that test.
A crash, syntax error or timeout fails only the affected test; remaining tests are still scored.
INNER JOIN naturally excludes securities without filled trades.
Notional uses quantity * price per row before summing.

questions.walkthrough: Filled trades only. MSFT: 200 × 410.30 + 100 × 411.10 = 82,060 + 41,110 = 123,170 (2 trades). JPM: 300 × 195.10 = 58,530. AAPL: 100 × 180.15 + 50 × 181.10 = 18,015 + 9,055 = 27,070 (the cancelled trade 12 is ignored). NVDA: 10 × 870.50 = 8,705. AMGN has no filled trades, so the INNER JOIN leaves it out.
hints: You need both tables: JOIN Trades to Securities on security_id.
Notional is quantity * price for each trade — put the multiplication inside SUM(...).
Filter FILLED trades in WHERE, GROUP BY the security, ROUND(SUM(...), 2), then ORDER BY total_notional DESC, ticker.

questions.statement:
Add two new columns to the trades table **without loops**:

* `notional = qty * price`
* `signed_qty = qty` for BUY trades and `-qty` for SELL trades

Return the columns `trade_id, side, qty, price, notional, signed_qty` in the original row order.
questions.starterCode:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def add_notional(trades: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    out = trades.copy()
    # TODO
    return out
questions.outputSpec: Columns [trade_id, side, qty, price, notional float64, signed_qty int64]; original row order.

comparison.dtypePolicy: Values compared by category: numeric (int/float interchangeable), bool, datetime, str; nulls (NaN/NaT/None/pd.NA) equal each other.

solution.referenceSolution:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def add_notional(trades):
    out = trades.copy()
    out["notional"] = out["qty"] * out["price"]
    out["signed_qty"] = np.where(out["side"] == "BUY", out["qty"], -out["qty"])
    return out[["trade_id", "side", "qty", "price", "notional", "signed_qty"]]
solution.explanation: Column arithmetic is vectorised: qty * price multiplies row by row. np.where(condition, a, b) chooses between two arrays element-wise, so BUY keeps qty and SELL gets -qty.

solution.referenceSolution:
import pandas as pd

def fill_gaps(trades):
    out = trades.copy()
    out["price"] = out["price"].fillna(out.groupby("ticker")["price"].transform("mean"))
    out["qty"] = out["qty"].fillna(0).astype("int64")
    return out[["trade_id", "ticker", "side", "qty", "price"]]
